# Compatibility Catalog Dual-State Incident Postmortem

This anomaly was not an extra old record appearing in the catalog, but the same name returning different current revision values at two viewing times. The original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause were not merged into a single "current state description", because the three respectively preserved object relationships at different times, a path that later proved recoverable, and a change whose cause had not been identified. Collapsing them into a single current page would make it impossible to revisit the initial divergence.

The compatibility catalog carries forward the public contracts established by compat, the migration records, and caller compatibility. It has its own schedule, maintenance arrangements, and exit conditions. Matching names are no substitute for determining provenance: a name can appear both in a legacy adoption relationship and at the current entry point, and these two records do not necessarily lead back to the same revision. The scope of this postmortem therefore covers catalog object relationships, not implementation-level attribution in adjacent projects.

## Initial Observations

The first observation was that the vendor alias did not match the old record. At first, this discrepancy only showed that the displayed content had changed, not whether the change was in the alias, the catalog record, or the object's source. Subsequent comparisons revealed a more specific phenomenon: the current entry point returned different revision values at two points in time. At that point, there was no basis for deciding which one should be called the "correct object", nor was either revision directly treated as a stale result.

Two preservation steps were taken at the time.

- The original record was retained along with the entry-point version at the time, as material from when the discrepancy was first observed.
- The fixture recovery page was saved separately, rather than replacing the original record with the recovered page.

Stopping further retries did not mean the issue was considered resolved. Once the entry point is refreshed, the page will show only the refreshed state; if the revision initially seen has not been preserved, it will be impossible to distinguish between "the object relationships once diverged" and "the page later recovered". Likewise, the recovery page can show that a recoverable path exists, but it cannot rewrite the entry point seen earlier, nor can it explain why deprecation changed.

The initial version deliberately kept several judgments separate: vendor alias was the starting point for comparison; different current revision values were the phenomenon that needed explanation; the fixture being recoverable was a local result; there was no conclusion on whether the old relationship had disappeared or on responsibility for long-term maintenance. This distinction remained valid later.

## The Impact Is Not the Page Text Itself

Changes to catalog text feed into callers' judgments about objects. If migration records are merged by matching names, different revision values may be made to look as though they share a single source; if callers see only the recovered entry point, they may continue to act on legacy adoption relationships; if the public contract retains only the latest page, it too will lose the material needed to explain existing adoption relationships.

Therefore, this page retains only one impact assessment: the provenance clues, migration records, and caller compatibility in the catalog were affected by the dual state. The material provides no customer list, request volume, service interruption duration, or production error rate, and this postmortem does not invent an impact scope to fill the gap. There is also no material indicating that compat itself failed, or that a change in an adjacent project caused the catalog discrepancy.

"The same object has two states" also does not predefine two stable categories for the two revision values. The point here is that the current entry point under the same name did not yield the same object determination when actually viewed. If one of them were immediately labeled the wrong object, the recovery page would be misread as the sole truth; if the two were immediately labeled independent objects, that would skip over the fact that the provenance chain had not yet been aligned.

## Changes over Time in Subsequent Records

After the initial version, the related work gradually broke "same name but inconsistent" down into provenance, adoption, environmental constraints and exit verification. The table below only lists how the recorded actions contribute to this retrospective, and does not treat card statuses as a complete account of events.

| Time | Recorded action or record | Impact on the assessment |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-11-25 | ICALA-001 completed the caller walkthrough | Began tracing provenance through callers and revisions, rather than guessing the object from the displayed text. |
| 2025-11-26 | ICALA-001 changed the assignee because the issue lay in another part of the implementation | Follow-up moved elsewhere; this was not a decision on long-term ownership of compatibility catalog maintenance. |
| 2025-12-11 morning | ICALA-012 was blocked because the CI queue was stuck | Local results were temporarily not used for further catalog assessments. |
| 2025-12-11 evening | ICALA-010 was blocked because the caller's account lacked permissions in that environment | The checks could not get past the required entry point; this does not establish that the object had been withdrawn. |
| 2025-12-11 later | ICALA-010 noted that the expiration action still pointed to the object from yesterday | The relationship to the old object was still affecting the action; looking only at the current display is not enough. |
| 2025-12-12 | ICALA-010 Switched the expiration action back to the original object, rather than following yesterday's screenshot | Object identification returned to the original record and source comparison. |
| 2025-12-12 | ICALA-012 Moved from blocked back to pending | The queue restriction was lifted, but a conclusion about the source did not automatically emerge. |
| 2025-12-30 | ICALA-021 Confirmed the scope of the exit action | Whether the old edge disappeared was listed as a separate check. |
| 2025-12-31 | Still at the exit entry point after switching accounts or workspaces | The exit check has not yet obtained a result for the old edge. |

The 12/11 statement "still points to yesterday's object" is not a root-cause conclusion. It only indicates that the expiration action does not match the object being processed. Switching back to the original object the next day does not declare that the original object is permanently correct either; this action rejects letting yesterday's screenshot continue to determine the object's identity. Taken together, the two records require the time of display, the source object available for review, and the actual target of the expiration action to be stored separately.

These three may sometimes refer to the same object, but they cannot be assumed to be the same just because their names match. Otherwise, display changes will rewrite the source, the source will in turn rewrite the exit action, and incorrect relationships will become locked in during a single cleanup pass. The dual-state anomaly persists not because it lacks a prettier name, but because these relationships were collapsed under a single name in the initial records.

## The Questions Answered by Each of the Four Types of Material

The original record preserves the current revision observed at a particular point in time. It is a clue for tracing the source, not an indication that it remained the current object later. The entry record from another point in time shows that an entry with the same name once resolved to a different revision; it cannot by itself prove that the two relationships have the same source. The recovery page shows that a recovery path exists for the fixture; it does not explain why the original discrepancy occurred. The vendor alias discrepancy was the earliest clue that prompted the comparison, not the final attribution.

| Material | What it can establish | What it cannot substitute for |
|---|---|---|
| Original record | The relationship between the entry first observed and its revision | The later current state or exit outcome |
| Entry at another point in time | Entries with the same name did in fact differ | Proof that the two entries share the same source |
| Recovery page | The fixture can return to a usable path | The cause of the original divergence |
| vendor alias differences | Where the comparison starts | Attribution of object relationships in the catalog |
| Expiry action record | The action once pointed to yesterday's object | A conclusion that the old edge has already been removed |

This table is not intended to divide the material into multiple incidents. It prevents one partial result from overriding another partial fact. If only the original record were retained, readers would think the recovery path had never appeared; if only the recovery page were retained, readers would think the catalog had never made a different determination about the objects; if only the expiry action were retained, the deviation in the action would in turn be misread as the cause of the source differences.

## From Alias Differences to Source Separation

The change in the vendor alias once led to a more limited explanation: the display text had changed, and the old record had not yet been synchronized. This explanation is retained in the initial account, because it was indeed the first change observed; but subsequent comparisons revealed different current revision values, not just different labels. The role of the alias differences in this version has therefore been narrowed to a point of comparison, and they can no longer serve as the basis for determining the cause.

Another premature conclusion was "the fixture has recovered, so the problem lies only in the test data". The recovery page shows that one path is usable again; the original record shows that different object relationships had existed. The two do not conflict, nor can they invalidate each other. After the fixture recovers, source tracing, adopter identification and exit actions must still be completed separately.

The approach in ICALA-001 is to follow the revision of `icalendar-compatibility-catalog` back to the earliest reconstructable source, rather than guessing the object from the display text in the catalog. This approach answers which object a revision can be traced back to. ICALA-010 instead require separating the current entry instances with the same name, so that the source and adopters are recorded separately for each of the two entries, rather than merging them by name. The former handles the source chains, while the latter prevents those source chains from being prematurely collapsed into one in the records.

When handling entries with the same name, the sequence should preserve specific object relationships, rather than treating a page screenshot as object identity: first identify which entry is being handled; then retain the revision observed for that entry; next link that revision to a source that can be reviewed; finally record the adopters separately. If the entry has not been identified, the name cannot stand in for it; if the source has not been reviewed, the recovered state cannot fill the gap; if the adopters are unknown, similar names cannot be used to infer who will be affected.

This is not an abstract set of migration steps, but a sequence determined by the misleading cues already encountered in this incident. Identical names encourage merging, yesterday's screenshot diverted the expiration action from its original object, and the recovery page is easily taken to mean that the overall relationship has been restored. Keeping separate records by entry, revision, source, and adopter means that display changes can only be treated as phenomena awaiting explanation, and cannot be used to directly rewrite object relationships.

## CI Queues and account permissions are two different constraints

ICALA-012 was blocked on 12 11 because the CI queue was stuck, and the local results were not used any further at the time. This constraint governs whether local results can be used in assessing the catalog. The card returned to pending on 12 12, meaning that the queue constraint was no longer blocking this work; it does not automatically turn earlier results into conclusions about the source, nor does it fill in the respective adopters for entries with the same name.

The blocker for ICALA-010 was different: the account provided by the caller lacked permissions in that environment, so the check could not reach the required entry. This result constrains whether the exit point can be reached. It does not mean that "the object has been withdrawn," nor that "permissions are the sole root cause." Switching accounts or workspaces might change whether operations can continue, but cannot explain the result observed in the restricted environment at the time.

Grouping both constraints under "access issues" would lose a key distinction. Queue recovery does not grant permissions; changing accounts does not automatically validate local results that have not yet been associated with an entry, either. Both are retained in the postmortem so that subsequent checks can identify which stage was left unfinished, not so that the two blockers can be recorded together as the cause of the anomaly.

## Boundaries of fixture recovery

The fact that the fixture can be restored is a positive result established in this incident. It rules out the conclusion that "this fixture path cannot be restored at all," but does not rule out the conclusion that "the two current entry instances are already consistent." The recovery page should not overwrite the original record, nor should the original record, in turn, negate the recovery result.

The practical value of retaining both pages is that later viewers can see two facts at the same time: there was a divergence in catalog relationships at one point in time; at another point, the fixture could be restored. If this is condensed to "everything is normal now," the original entry version will be lost; if only the anomalous state is retained, people will instead be misled into thinking there is no recovery path.

The recovery result also cannot replace exit verification. Fixture recovery addresses whether a path can be returned to a usable state; the exit action addresses whether the old relationship still remains in the catalog and in adoption relationships. Even if both occur in the same round of work, they have different completion criteria. Nothing in the material here supports treating the success of one as completion of the other.

In the following situations, continuing to refresh the entry will only create new page states, without adding facts needed for this postmortem:

- The current entry repeatedly displays one of the revisions, but no new source material has been added;
- The page has changed, but the earliest version of the entry that was seen was not retained;
- Operations can continue after switching accounts or workspaces, but this does not explain where they stopped in the original restricted environment;
- After the CI queue was restored only local results were available, and they still could not be linked to the catalog entry;
- After the fixture was restored an attempt was made to directly record the old relationship as withdrawn.

Stopping at these points does not mean abandoning the checks. It separates the restoration results already obtained from the source information, adopter information and exit results that have not been obtained. Without new material on object relationships, repeatedly refreshing the current page will not make the two revisions naturally become the same object.

## Exit Actions and Verification of Old Edges

ICALA-021 covers replaying the withdrawal, and checking whether the old edge has actually disappeared. This scope is stricter than "the page has already been updated", but does not go beyond the available material. The catalog display may change first, while the old relationship may still remain with adopters, in expiration actions or in recovery page references; conversely, even if the old relationship is eventually removed, this cannot explain why two current revisions appeared in the first place.

Exit checks have at least two mutually independent outcomes: whether the exit action reaches the entry point, and whether the old edge has disappeared. The former may be cut short by account or workspace restrictions; the latter can only be answered when the old relationship can actually be checked. "Stopped at the exit entry point" cannot substitute for "the old edge is still present", nor can the fact that the old edge has not yet been verified be used to deny that the fixture has been restored.

The record from day 31 of month 12 illustrates exactly this boundary. After switching accounts or workspaces, the operation still stopped at the exit entry point. It did not prove that the exit entry point was broken, nor did it prove that the withdrawal had failed. It only records that this check did not get past the entry point, so the old edge verification produced no result. If this stopping point is recorded as either a success or a failure, a conclusion would be supplied for a check that never took place.

When replaying the withdrawal, first confirm which current entry is being handled and its source, then inspect the adopter relationships retained by that entry, and then check whether the expiration action still points to the original object. If it is possible to get past the exit entry point, only then check whether the old edge has disappeared. If the operation stops at the entry point, simply record where it stopped, without treating this as a successful or failed withdrawal.

There is a clear historical reason for this order: the expiration action was once led astray by yesterday's object. If the current display is examined first, and the source is traced afterward, a new screenshot may once again become the material used to determine the object's identity. With the entry, source and adopter separated first, display changes cannot directly drive the exit action.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Original record retained
    Original record retained --> Same-name discrepancy found
    Same-name discrepancy found --> Entry point sources separated
    Entry point sources separated --> fixture restored
    Entry point sources separated --> Cause unconfirmed
    fixture restored --> Exit relationship verification
    Cause unconfirmed --> Exit relationship verification
    Exit relationship verification --> Old edge has disappeared
    Exit relationship verification --> Stopped at the exit entry point
```

In the diagram, "Old edge has disappeared" is the result that exit verification should establish, not a fact already confirmed in this incident. "Stopped at the exit entry point" is the state already recorded during the incident. Recovery, source separation, and exit verification are placed on different branches so that a page being recoverable, object sources being distinguishable, and old relationships having been withdrawn are no longer conflated.

## Gaps in the maintenance arrangements

ICALA-012 only lists the temporary assignee for the current action, while the long-term owner responsible for maintaining the entry point was still unknown at the time. The assignee change on day 26 of month 11 was because the issue lay in another part of the implementation, not a final allocation of long-term maintenance responsibility for the compatibility directory. Neither piece of evidence is sufficient to establish a permanent maintainer in this postmortem.

At this stage, three types of responsibility can be reliably retained: preserving the coexistence of the original record, the restored page, and the unconfirmed cause; keeping track of the respective sources and consumers of the two entry points with the same name; replaying the withdrawal and checking the old edge when it becomes possible to get past the exit entry point. Long-term maintenance ownership still needs to be confirmed within the existing maintenance arrangements. Writing up the temporary handoff, card adjustments, and long-term responsibility as a single conclusion would leave no reference point for reviewing the next entry point change.

The compatibility directory's separate schedule was not canceled because of this anomaly. The anomaly affected object assessments in compat's public contract, migration records, and caller compatibility; the available materials do not indicate that implementation changes in adjacent projects should be incorporated into this page. This postmortem records the directory object's dual state, recovery results, source separation, and exit boundary, and does not make causal determinations for other projects.

DOC-32 holds the exit-window checklist. This page only explains why the dual state requires separate verification of exit relationships, and does not reproduce the execution details in the exit checklist. ICALA-001, ICALA-010, ICALA-012, and ICALA-021 retain navigation for source review, separation of same-named entry points, queue and temporary handoff constraints, and the scope of exit actions, respectively.

## Explanations still unconfirmed

There is currently no answer as to why deprecation changed. The facts supported by the existing material are: vendor alias was first observed to differ from the old record; the current entry at two points in time showed different revisions; fixture can be restored; the expiration action once pointed to yesterday's object; the CI queue and account permissions each previously restricted checks; after the account or workspace was changed, it still stopped at the exit entry. These facts make up the sequence of events, but are insufficient to explain which of them caused the change.

The following claims still cannot be treated as conclusions:

- the change in deprecation was necessarily caused by vendor alias;
- the difference between the two revisions came only from screenshots or caches;
- restoring fixture proves that the directory source never diverged;
- switching the expiration action back to the original object proves that the old edge has disappeared;
- after the CI queue was unblocked, all prior local results could be used directly to assess the directory;
- if changing the account or workspace still leaves it at the exit entry, permissions can be concluded to be the only constraint.

Each of these judgments bypasses at least one of source, exit, environment, or timing. Leaving the cause unknown is not leaving the anomaly stuck in place; it avoids forming a more easily propagated incorrect version after recovery.

If additional material appears later, prioritize adding relationships that could change the object assessment: the confirmed source of a particular current entry, the correspondence between an adopter and an entry, the result of checking the old edge after the exit action has crossed the entry, or a record that can connect the change in deprecation to its relationship with a specific object. Display screenshots without a source, claims based on memory that same-named objects were merged, success pages borrowed from adjacent projects, and listing a temporary takeover person as the long-term maintainer cannot change the judgments already made on this page.

What can currently be confirmed is that fixture can be restored; what clearly needs to be stored separately is the source and adopter of the same-named current entry; what still needs to be checked is whether the old relationship truly disappeared after the exit action; what remains open is the reason for the change in deprecation. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause continue to coexist, because if any one of them is deleted, people viewing it later can only see the organized current state and cannot reconstruct why the same object once appeared in two states.

# Compatibility Directory Exit Window Checklist

The compatibility directory window can be used to roll back temporary actions, but cannot replace release sign-off. When closing the window, answer only three questions: whether the exit actions are complete, what the last visible result was, and whether adj-icalendar itself still has a bypass in place that will continue to affect the entry point. All other release decisions still require separate confirmation from the respective owner.

The designated entry point is `docs/adj-icalendar/release/icalendar-compatibility-catalog-exit-window-checklist.md`. When entering from the current revision, first confirm that both the page and its attachments still open; do not treat a page as the current entry point just because an old bookmark still takes you to it. ICALA-019 is used to record the first broken link on these paths. ICALA-030 is only for finding an adjacent revision with a working path and checking where the paths first differ. Neither card establishes that the window can be closed.

## Window Opening Record

- [ ] Record the `component` being handled, the current revision, and why exit actions are needed this time. Do not add background on objects outside the directory here.
- [ ] Keep the raw results for one of the project's own success paths and one rejection path. The results should show where the input ended up; do not substitute a "success" in the aggregate logs.
- [ ] After running `release probe`, keep its original output alongside this record. If the probe has already changed the directory contents or entry-point state, note whether that happened before or after the sample was captured.
- [ ] First check whether the entry point for the current revision is reachable. Record the first broken-link location in ICALA-019; if no entry point is reachable, do not switch to a similarly named historical page to continue closing the window.

The old version only required seeing `round trip` before continuing. That is not enough. It did not distinguish between "a result exists" and "the entry point is still accepting new work after exit." This version retains that old practice as a reminder: it is suitable for confirming that output was left behind at the time, but not as the sole basis for exit.

## Exit Actions

1. Check against the window opening record and confirm that there is a last visible result for `round trip`. If that is missing, stop: do not remove the bypass or mark the work complete.
2. Check the artifact or state of `content-line`. If all you can see is a success message in the logs, keep the window open, because that does not confirm what was actually left on the directory side.
3. Remove the temporary bypass added for this window, then access the entry point again from the current revision. If the entry point is unreachable, preserve the broken-link location first; if an adjacent revision has a working path, compare only the first point where the paths differ, and do not mix content from subsequent pages into these results.
4. Confirm that no new work continues to pass through that bypass after removal. If new work is still coming in, restore the bypass, record the last result visible at that time, and leave the window open.

Here, "restore the bypass" is meant to prevent its removal from cutting off directory processing that is still in progress; it does not mean reverting to any old release version. After restoring it, you must start checking again from the window opening record; you cannot directly reuse the `round trip` from before restoration as the new exit result.

## Two Stop Conditions

**Broken entry-point link.** If the entry point for the current revision does not open, or is accessible only through an old link, stop at the first broken link. ICALA-019 records the location encountered by an actual consumer entering from the current revision. If an adjacent revision is needed as a reference, record it in ICALA-030; the reference only shows path differences and does not prove that the current page has been fixed.

**Someone has taken over, but long-term ownership is unclear.** ICALA-028 can record the temporary assignee for the action being taken. It does not change long-term ownership of the maintenance entry point. The handoff record should clearly state whether to keep the bypass in place, wait for the entry point to be restored, or capture samples again; without that statement, the window still counts as open.

## Window Closure Record

- [ ] Keep the raw result of the last success or rejection, and note whether it occurred before or after bypass removal.
- [ ] Record that the bypass has been removed, or state why it was restored. Do not use "handled" as the only result.
- [ ] If the current entry point has a broken link, preserve the first location and link to ICALA-019; do not put speculation about anything beyond the broken link into the exit record.
- [ ] If the temporary assignee continues the work, update the current action in ICALA-028; leave the long-term maintenance entry point unchanged if it is still undetermined.

ICALA-008 is an early baseline and a record of shift handoffs, useful for looking back at who previously handled the entry point; it cannot replace checks on the current revision. For windows that have been rolled back, the records should contain at least the samples from window opening, the last visible result, and the bypass's final state. If any one of these is missing, treat the work as incomplete and retain the restoration action.

# Alternative Proposal for the Compatibility Catalog

This proposal remains in the working draft for `adj-icalendar` and discusses how `icalendar-compatibility-catalog` should hold compatibility information. It does not present the trial as a rule already in effect.

There were two options at the time. Option one was to keep organizing content around the `compatibility` entry point: the name would carry over, existing readers would not need to switch entry points, and changes would be small; the trade-off was that old and new catalogs could easily get mixed together, and old links might overwrite entries still in use. Option two was to split `downstream client` out on its own, keeping only compatibility relationships and sources in the catalog and leaving each caller to maintain its own adoption results. This option had clearer boundaries, but the existing callers of `parser trace` had not yet been confirmed, and splitting the entry points would also require an additional migration.

Objections centered on "who would maintain aliases after the split" and "whether entry points with the same name would be merged back together." `vendor alias` was left in place at the time; there was not enough material to decide whether it belonged in the catalog or with the caller. Observations of `alarm` were also only partial records, not a basis for deciding the overall catalog approach.

If the second option is tried first, the two entry points must, at a minimum, be distinguishable by revision before the trial, with the source and adopters recorded for each; ordinary old links must not overwrite new entries. # Freeze Window Decision Record

## Two Approaches Left on the Table

R2026.09 The freeze window discussion was about whether the boundary should move, not about changing a single implementation detail. The current entry point has already been used for this round's search and regression; the other proposal was to adjust the window so that changes to the typed-values entry point would enter freeze along with this round. The two approaches had different implications at the time:

| Approach | Direct impact visible at the time | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current typed-values entry point | Continue regression over the range already investigated, without proactively expanding the freeze boundary | Adopted |
| Adjust the window | Entry-point changes and downstream compatibility would need to be checked together; the existing materials did not cover the full impact | Not adopted |

Adopting the first approach does not mean that the current entry point has been permanently assigned. It only means that during R2026.09, the entry point will not be moved proactively, and the range already known will be fixed first. Adjusting the window remains in the decision record; if it is proposed again later, the actual impact and compatibility consequences must be reintroduced.

## Trade-offs Discussed in the Meeting

The main benefit of retaining the current entry point is that it keeps the regression gate within the range already investigated. This does not require an unconfirmed entry-point change to be written as an established part of freeze, nor does it prematurely treat the impact that downstream users Fang Ke might experience as already having occurred. For this round, keeping the scope contained is easier to roll back than advancing two changes at the same time.

Adjusting the window was not judged to be the wrong direction. The reason for opposing it was specific: at the time, the materials covered only the entry point and the lookup location; there was no sufficient actual-impact record showing which downstream consumers would be affected after the adjustment, where the compatibility consequences would appear, or whether those consequences could be identified in this round of regression. A call name or a file location cannot replace this confirmation.

The meeting materials constrained this trade-off with the following principle:

> Treat the frozen repository and its public parser behavior as the authority; every claim travels with a reproducible input, source path, and downstream compatibility consequence.

In the context of this page, this sentence requires the decision to follow the reproducible input, source path, and downstream compatibility consequence. It supports retaining the entry point that has already been investigated, and it also limits writing the window adjustment as an approved matter. It does not supply a compatibility conclusion for the entry-point change that did not exist at the time.

## Boundary Actually Enforced Within freeze

This round continues to use the current typed-values entry point as the boundary for regression work. Coordination focuses on two areas: handing the approved scope over to the regression gate, and documenting the window adjustment that was not adopted and the reasons for not adopting it. core-06 is the coordination entry point on the quality side, but this coordination does not establish long-term maintenance ownership of the entry point.

The old entry point has not been deleted from the record. Keeping it serves two practical purposes: first, when window adjustments are discussed again later, comparisons can still start from the original entry point; second, if the adjustment is withdrawn, it will be possible to identify what this round's freeze actually froze. Here, "reversible" means that the records and boundaries can still be revisited, not that a switchover operation is already prepared.

The location found by following `src/icalendar/attr.py` is also retained. This path shows where the investigation started at the time, not that the file is the permanent home, and certainly cannot on its own determine who should be responsible for compatibility issues after the entry point changes. The relationship between the path and the entry point can serve as a starting point for review, but that starting point cannot be extended into an ownership conclusion.

## Review Addendum

A later review revisited the file location and the name used in calls. The review could confirm that the lookup still points to `src/icalendar/attr.py`, and that it was treated as the lookup destination for the current entry point at the time; the review did not uncover new evidence sufficient to change the freeze choice. The original decision therefore remains in place: no window adjustment for R2026.09, and first complete this round's in-scope regression testing through the current typed-values entry point.

This additional check did not elevate the "entry point location" into a "permanent maintenance boundary". Likewise, without seeing new downstream compatibility results, a window adjustment cannot be recast as a settled action that is safe and feasible. The review changed the clarity of the record, not the scope approved at the time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Identified scope"] --> B["Keep the current typed-values entry point"]
    A --> C["Adjust the window"]
    B --> D["R2026.09 freeze"]
    C --> E["Not adopted"]
```

## Reservations

The unresolved matters left by this decision have defined boundaries. The actual impact of adjusting the entry point on downstream compatibility remains unconfirmed in the materials for this round; `src/icalendar/attr.py` remains only a lookup path and cannot be used to establish permanent ownership. Neither of these two matters has automatically become a settled fact simply because of the decision to "keep the current entry point".

If the adjustment window is reopened in the future, the new actual impact, reproducible inputs, source paths, and compatibility consequences need to be considered together before deciding whether to move the boundary. What can be confirmed from this page alone is: R2026.09 freeze chose not to move the current entry point, and retained the alternatives that were not adopted and the reasons for not adopting them.

This is also why the old entry point needs to remain in the record. Deleting it would leave future readers seeing only "keep the current entry point", without seeing that adjusting the window had also been weighed at the time, or why entry point changes were not addressed in the same round. The record preserves the point in time when that choice was made, but does not sanitize it into a permanent rule that still applies today.

This review did not combine every hit for typed-values, interop, and office hours into a single relationship graph. Those terms can appear near each other; matching names do not establish a handoff between objects. This page keeps a short route that someone taking over can retrace: start at the public entry point for typed-values, select one direct caller, and follow that call into interop office hours. The first consumer that actually receives the call is the endpoint of this check.

`src/icalendar/attr.py` is still a file along the route. Previously, we could trace back to the object and call names here, so it is a useful place to look again for clues near the entry point. It is not the fixed home of office hours, and its filename, directory location, or similar symbols cannot be used to infer the next call in the chain. Locating code near the entry point and identifying the collaboration entry point are two different things; keep them distinct when reading the code.

```text
[typed-values public entry point]
            |
            | One selected direct call
            v
[Direct caller]
            |
            | Enter interop office hours
            v
[First actual consumer]
            |
            +-- Stop if an explanation requires another owner

rollback marker --> Revisit a previous backtrack point
Same-name files with no call edge --> Landmarks only
```

Only the public entry point counts as the start of the route. Wrappers, aliases, and descriptive names in search results can help you tell whether you are still in the same area, but they do not automatically become the next step after the entry point. First confirm the object to trace at the entry point, then find one direct caller of it; do not work backward from a seemingly related file to infer who calls it. This keeps the scope small, but avoids writing up "similar names" as "a call exists."

Choose only one direct caller as well. This is not a complete call inventory for typed-values; it is meant to leave an actual entry point into office hours. Once a caller is selected, keep all subsequent observations focused on that one call: where it is handed off and where it is received. If several callers are included at once, the next person will not be able to tell which branches have been checked and which are just adjacent hits on the search page; during handoff, a side path can also easily be misreported as the entry into office hours.

After entering office hours, find the first actual consumer. This term has a clear boundary: it means only that the selected call has reached a real receiving point. It does not cover all processing after that consumer, or identify the overall entry point for the entire interop mechanism. The earlier draft was too brief on this point, making it easy to assume the trace should continue to the final handler. Following the review, the stopping point is explicit: answering "Where does typed-values enter this shared processing?" is enough. Open a separate question for what happens after that.

The rollback marker should be read alongside the call chain, not attached below it. It records where this path previously doubled back and is useful to revisit when you encounter inconsistent names or locations. It can remind readers to check whether this call segment still passes through the same area, and help explain why some old traces remain nearby; on its own, it cannot prove that the consumer is still in its original location, much less replace confirmation of an actual call. Keeping the marker lets people coming later see this history, instead of mistakenly deleting traces of a rollback as though it had never happened.

Files with the same name but no call edge are simpler to handle: keep them as landmarks, outside the diagram's main line. For example, if a search turns up another object containing typed-values or the word interop, you can use it as a sign that you are near the same topic; the next step should still be to return to the selected direct caller and confirm who it actually hands off to. These files are useful for finding your bearings again, but are not enough to identify the "first consumer." Mixing the two kinds of material usually sends the route off course from the start.

When actually retracing the route, keep this order:

1. Confirm the current object at the public entry point for typed-values.
2. Follow only one direct caller; do not add branches based on same-name results.
3. Find the first actual consumer in interop office hours.
4. Treat the rollback marker as a point to revisit, and record it separately from the current call.
5. If explaining the next destination requires another owner, stop at that consumer.

These steps do not require listing every related file. The public entry point establishes the start, the direct caller fixes the object being observed, the first consumer identifies where office hours actually receives the call, and the marker preserves the historical location. Together, they are enough for the person taking over to start from the same place without presenting unconfirmed downstream processing as an established relationship.

The location of `attr.py`, the rollback marker, and same-name files cannot answer that question. # On-call rotation window mismatch postmortem

During the rotation window, the visible on-call assignment did not match the original plan. No operational anomalies were noticed during the initial handoff; the confirmed mismatch was in coordination: someone was still handling items within the window according to the original plan, and only later noticed that the displayed on-call assignment was already different. This record covers only the plan, handoff, and temporary recovery; it does not classify this as a service incident.

The confirmed impact was that, for a time, it was unclear who the on-call coordinator was, and both the original plan and the window results were being used to make decisions. The team actually had two visible references, not one entry point that was already invalid and another that was clearly valid. The old entry point was still usable, so it was not disabled immediately; this left room for recovery and gave the team another reversible option. The scope of the actual impact was not explored further at the time, and no basis was recorded for making changes to anything outside the rotation as a result.

The sequence recorded during the window was:

- Before the window began, everyone prepared for handoff according to the original plan; no discrepancy had been seen yet.
- When the mismatch was first noticed, the comparison was between the result visible at that point and the original plan. The mismatch was confirmed only in this instance; it was not taken at the time to mean that the same problem had already occurred in other windows.
- The temporary recovery did not rearrange the entire rotation. Instead, the old entry point was retained and the coordinator continued under the original plan; the old entry point could be withdrawn.
- After recovery, the round-trip fixture was retained for later review of the discrepancy at the time, rather than treating the temporary action as an explanation of the cause.

The assessment at the time was to give the round-trip side lower priority because the fixture had not reliably reproduced the mismatch seen in the window. This was just the team's investigation order, not a root-cause conclusion. That assessment continued to be cited later because it explained why recovery did not wait for a full diagnosis; this passage should not be read as "the fixture has been ruled out." The team also did not establish a chain of evidence that would justify closing the investigation: what was confirmed was that the plan and the displayed result did not match; what remained unconfirmed was whether the divergence occurred at handoff, in the display, or during coordination.

The coordinator needs to confirm two things before the next handoff: who will receive the window results, and when the old entry point will be withdrawn. The former is the gap this mismatch directly exposed; if the original plan and the visible result continue to guide actions independently, the next shift will face the same conflict in deciding what to follow. The latter is what keeps the temporary recovery from quietly becoming the usual path. This record provides no long-term arrangement for either item and no basis for concluding that a permanent fix has been completed.

The open questions remain: where the original plan and the window results began to diverge, whether the discrepancy occurred only in this round, and whether the same mismatch will surface again after the old entry point is withdrawn. Without those answers, the temporary recovery cannot be written up as a permanent fix. If all we see next time is that the results line up again, that only indicates a surface-level recovery in the window; it cannot by itself show which of the round-trip fixture, the old entry point, or the handoff sequence caused the change.

# CI Image Result Discrepancy Troubleshooting Tree

During verification, treat "complete" on the ticket only as a claim to check. First record the entry point used to invoke component-api and its version in one place; where the entry point comes from and whether the version matches form the first branch point. Once the live check reaches this point, compare the parser traces for the same input side by side. The two traces are not a substitute for evidence from the image itself.

```text
Results still can't be verified
├─ Either the entry point or the version doesn't match
│  └─ Record the actual entry point and the version observed. Don't use results from another build to fill in the conclusion; stop.
└─ Both the entry point and version match
   ├─ parser traces differ
   │  └─ Record the actual impact, coordinator, and the old entry point that can be withdrawn; hand off to whoever needs to provide the image evidence, and stop here.
   └─ parser traces match, but conclusions still differ
      └─ The image evidence needed to account for the difference has not yet been obtained. Leave it blank; don't keep rerunning.
```

Here, "the same input" means the very same input passed to the parser, not two tasks that look similar. If the inputs have not been confirmed to be identical, do not enter the trace branch; return to the entry point and version. Don't substitute a statement that the refresh is complete for these two checks.

This verification did not conclude from the discrepancy that the refresh had taken effect, nor did it classify the discrepancy as a problem with component-api. Leave the record fields blank for now: actual impact ___; coordinator ___; whether the old entry point can be withdrawn ___. If a point requiring a new owner comes up first, leave these fields blank and do not investigate further.
